story1355:
In the time before time, Rangi the Sky Father lay pressed close against Papa the Earth Mother, and between them they held all their children in a dark, warm embrace. Their children—the gods of forest, sea, wind, and war—existed in cramped blackness, unable to move or see. Among them were Tane Mahuta, god of forests and birds; Tangaroa, god of the sea; Tawhiri Matea, god of winds and storms; Haumia-tiketike, god of wild food; Rongo, god of cultivated food and peace; and Tu, god of war. Each child longed for space, for light, for the world above.

The brothers gathered in council to discuss their plight. "Let us push our parents apart," said Tu, "so that we may live in the light." But the brothers disagreed on how far to separate them. Tane wanted gentle light and soft rain for the forests. Tangaroa wanted the sky far enough that tides would ebb and flow. Tawhiri wanted to remain close to his mother Rangi, to rage and weep against her body as storms.

Tane Mahuta pressed his great strength against Papa while Rangi pleaded with them to stop. When Tane finally thrust the Sky Father upward with his mighty back, light flooded the world for the first time. Rangi wept for her lost children, and her tears fell as rain upon the new land. Tawhiri, refusing to leave his mother, flew upward with her and became the storms that still rage between sky and earth. The other brothers settled on Papa's body and became the forests, the seas, the fertile ground, and the wild creatures.

Thus the world was born from separation and grief. The Maori say that even now, when the mist rises from the mountains on still mornings, it is Rangi's breath reaching down to embrace Papa once more, a love that separation could never fully destroy.
story1356:
Maui was a demigod of boundless cunning, born of the sea foam and raised by his grandmother Te Kahu-turanga. From childhood he showed supernatural gifts—shaping the world with his hands and his sharp mind. But it was his greatest fishing expedition that changed Aotearoa forever.

Maui and his brothers set out in their great waka hourua, the double-hulled canoe, sailing far into the Pacific. While his brothers fished normally, Maui fashioned a massive hook from the jawbone of his ancestor Muri-rangi-tohi, then chanted ancient karakia to summon the power of the deep. He cast his line into the ocean and felt something immense snag on his hook. The line went taut with a force that nearly pulled him overboard.

"Pull!" Maui shouted to his brothers, but they were frightened and refused. So Maui hooked the line to the gunwale of the canoe and began hauling alone. For days he pulled, his muscles burning, his voice chanting the incantations of the sea gods. Slowly, impossibly, the ocean floor began to rise. Coral reefs broke the surface. Mud and sand followed, then rock and forest.

The brothers, seeing land emerging, grew jealous and struck the rising earth with their paddles, creating the rough ridges and valleys that mark the North Island's spine. When Maui finally released his hook, it fell to earth and became the Kaingaroa Plains. The great fish he had pulled from the sea was Te Ika a Māui—the Fish of Maui—now known as the North Island of New Zealand. The South Island became the waka canoe, and Stewart Island the anchor stone.

The Maori say that earthquakes are caused by the great fish still trembling on Maui's hook, a reminder that the land itself was once a living creature pulled from the deep.
story1357:
Maui watched the sun race across the sky each day, far too quickly for the people to dry their nets, gather food, or weave their cloaks. His mother Hine-te-aeowho complained bitterly: "The sun moves so fast that my flax dries before I can beat it into cloth!" Maui resolved to slow the sun down.

He traveled to the eastern horizon where the sun, Tama-nui-te-ra, rose each morning, and he told his brothers to gather ropes of flax and harakeke, weaving them into massive snares. Then Maui and his brothers climbed Mount Hikurangi, the highest point where the sun first touches the earth, and set their traps in the sun's path.

When dawn came and the great sun began its daily arc, Maui sprang from hiding and cast his ropes. The first snare broke—Maui had underestimated the sun's strength. He tried again with a second, stronger snare, and this time it held. The sun was caught, blazing and furious, struggling against the flax ropes that burned but did not break.

Maui approached the sun with his weapon, the jawbone weapon of his ancestor, and struck the sun's rays one by one. He beat some longer, some shorter, until the sun agreed to slow its journey across the sky. "From now on," Maui told the sun, "you will race across the sky in summer when the days are long, and creep slowly in winter when the days are short."

The sun agreed, and from that day the seasons had their rhythm. The people could dry their food, weave their cloaks, and plant their gardens in the generous light. Mount Hikurangi remains sacred to the Ngāti Porou iwi, who say the sun still pauses there each morning, remembering its defeat at Maui's hands.
story1358:
Fire had been lost to the world, and the people suffered in cold and darkness. Maui learned from the old stories that fire was kept hidden by Mahuika, the goddess of fire, who dwelt at the edge of the underworld. Determined to steal fire for humanity, Maui journeyed to Mahuika's domain.

He found the fire goddess in her cave, her hair aflame, her eyes like burning coals. Maui approached with flattery and cunning, telling her of her own greatness and asking for a single flame to warm his old grandmother. Mahuika, pleased by his words, pulled a fingernail from her hand and tossed it to him—a flame blazed from the nail and raced across the dry grass, setting the forest alight.

Maui carried the fire away, but when he looked back, the flame had gone out. He returned to Mahuika and asked for another. She gave him another nail, and another, and each time the fire died before Maui could carry it far. Growing suspicious, Mahuika realized Maui was deceiving her. In rage, she hurled the last of her fire at Maui, but he dodged and leaped into a lake, the flames chasing him across the water.

Maui dove deep and called upon his ancestor, the great fish Te Tuna, to carry the fire safely through the waters. When he emerged, he carried fire in the heart of a green branch. He raced across the land, planting fire in the kioka and kahikatea trees, hiding it in the dry bark where humans would later strike sparks.

This is why, the Maori say, different trees hold fire differently—some burn hot and fast, others smolder gently. Maui had spread fire across all the trees so that humanity would never again be without warmth.
story1359:
After all his great deeds—fishing up the North Island, slowing the sun, stealing fire—Maui desired immortality for humankind. He knew that Hine-nui-te-po, the Great Lady of Night and goddess of death, held the secret of eternal life in her belly. If Maui could enter her sleeping body and remove the life-giving gem, death would be banished from the world forever.

Maui told his brothers his plan and set out for the realm of the spirits. He found Hine-nui-te-po sleeping on the shore of Rarohenga, the underworld, her body radiant with pale light, her mouth stretched wide like a cave. Maui instructed his brothers to watch silently and not to laugh, no matter what they saw.

With great courage, Maui approached the sleeping goddess and began to enter her body feet first. But as he crawled upward, the tiny birds of the forest—the piwakawaka fantail—fluttered around Maui's brothers and began to laugh. One brother could not help himself and burst into laughter. The sound woke Hine-nui-te-po.

The goddess opened her eyes and saw what Maui was doing. In fury, she seized him with her obsidian teeth and crushed him. Maui died instantly, and his body was cast down into the underworld.

From that day, death ruled the world. Maui's brothers returned to the land of the living and told the people that immortality had been lost forever. The Maori say this is why humans must die—because Maui's courage was undone by a brother's laughter, and the chance for eternal life was sealed forever within Hine-nui-te-po's body. Death, once a door that could have been closed, remained forever open.
story1360:
Kupe was a great navigator and chief of Hawaiki, the legendary homeland of the Maori. He sailed the vast Pacific in his great waka hourua, exploring islands and charting the stars with supernatural skill. But it was a monstrous creature of the deep that led him to Aotearoa.

A great taniwha—a sea serpent of immense size and malevolence—had taken up residence in the waters around Hawaiki, terrorizing fishermen and capsizing canoes. Kupe pursued the creature for months across the open ocean, his crew exhausted, his provisions dwindling. The taniwha was cunning, diving beneath the waves and resurfacing far ahead, but Kupe followed its wake with unerring precision.

The chase led Kupe south through unfamiliar waters, past islands of fire and islands of white coral, through storms and calm, until at last the taniwha surfaced in a bay sheltered by tall green mountains. Kupe struck the creature with his great patu, a weapon carved from greenstone, and killed it. He buried the taniwha's bones beneath the cliffs, and its body became the land that juts into the bay—now called the Palliser region.

Kupe looked upon the land he had discovered and saw that it was good. The forests were rich with birds, the rivers ran with fish, and the climate was warm and green. He named the land Aotearoa—the Land of the Long White Cloud—for the great cloud that hung over the mountains. He returned to Hawaiki and told his people of the new land, and many followed him south in great fleets of canoes.

The taniwha's bones still rest beneath the cliffs, and fishermen say that on stormy nights, the ghost of the sea serpent still lashes the waves.
story1361:
In the waters of what is now Wellington Harbour, two great taniwha lived—Ngake and Whataitai. They were ancient beings, serpentine and powerful, who had shaped the harbour from the soft earth and stone. Ngake was restless and fierce, while Whataitai was gentle and content.

One day, Ngake decided to leave the harbour and swim out to the open sea. With a great surge, he burst through the sandbar that separated the harbour from the ocean, carving the channel that would become the entrance to Port Nicholson. The rush of water was enormous, and the harbour emptied in a great tidal wave that reshaped the coastline.

Whataitai, too slow to follow, was stranded in the shallowing water. As the harbour dried and the land rose, Whataitai lay stranded on the flats, unable to return to the sea. The people of the harbour district say that Whataitai became the land itself—his great body forming the ridge that rises above the harbour flats. His bones became the rocks, his flesh the soil, and his spirit became the wind that sweeps across the harbour.

Ngake, meanwhile, roamed the open ocean, and some say he still lives in the deep waters beyond the Heads, occasionally surfacing to remind the people that the harbour was once his home. The harbour bears the scars of their parting—the narrow entrance carved by Ngake's desperate burst, the flat southern shore where Whataitai lay down and died.

The people who lived along the harbour's edge knew the story and respected the taniwha's domain. They warned their children not to swim alone in the deep channels, for Ngake might still be watching, and Whataitai's spirit might pull them down into the soft earth beneath the water.
story1362:
Hatupatu was a young man of great courage and restless spirit, living in a village beside a deep forest. He was the son of a chief, but he preferred the company of birds and trees to the ceremonies of the meeting house. One day, while hunting in the deep bush, he encountered something extraordinary—a bird-woman, a creature of terrible beauty, with feathers instead of hair and talons instead of fingers.

The bird-woman was Karura, a supernatural being of immense power. She captured Hatupatu and carried him away to her cave in the mountains, where she kept him as her prisoner and her pet. Hatupatu was terrified, but he was also clever. He learned the ways of the bird-woman, her habits, her weaknesses. He discovered that Karura could not bear the sound of certain birdsong, and he learned to mimic the call of the tui and the bellbird.

One day, when Karura was hunting far from the cave, Hatupatu escaped. He ran through the forest, mimicking birdsong to confuse the bird-woman when she returned and found him gone. Karura flew above the canopy, searching, but the bird calls confused her and she could not tell which sounds were real and which were Hatupatu's imitations.

Hatupatu reached his village and told his people of the bird-woman's cave. They armed themselves with greenstone clubs and sacred weapons, and they marched into the forest to confront Karura. When they found the cave, they set it ablaze, and Karura flew away screaming into the upper sky, never to return.

Hatupatu became a great chief, known for his wisdom and his courage. The birds of the forest still call his name, and the Maori say that when you hear the tui singing in the deep bush, it is Hatupatu calling to remind you that even the most fearsome enemy can be defeated by wit and patience.
story1363:
In the great thermal valley of Rotorua, two young lovers defied the boundaries of their people. Hinemoa was the daughter of a chief, beautiful and proud, living on the eastern shore of the lake. Tutanekai was the son of a rival chief, a skilled flute player who lived on Mokoia Island in the center of the lake. Their families forbade them from seeing each other, but at night, Tutanekai played his flute—his koauau—and the music drifted across the water to Hinemoa's ears.

The melody tormented Hinemoa with longing. She could not bear to be apart from Tutanekai, but the lake was wide and cold, and she had no canoe. One night, driven to desperation by the music, she walked to the shore, stripped off her clothes, and waded into the lake. The water was freezing, and the lake was deep, but Hinemoa swam with fierce determination, following the sound of Tutanekai's flute.

She swam through the night, her body numbing, her breath failing. Twice she nearly drowned, but each time the music pulled her forward. When she finally reached Mokoia Island, she collapsed on the shore, exhausted and shivering. Tutanekai found her there and wrapped her in his cloak. They built a fire and warmed themselves, and by morning, the chief and the people had accepted their union.

The fire they lit that morning became the great thermal spring that still burns on Mokoia Island, and the people named it Hinemoa's Pool. The story of their love is told every year at the festival of the lake, and the sound of the flute still carries across the water at night.
story1364:
In the time before humans, the mountains of the world moved and fought. Each mountain wanted to be the tallest, the most powerful, the most beautiful. They clashed and roared, their peaks scraping the sky, their roots tearing the earth. The forests were destroyed, the rivers were dammed, and the world was chaos.

Among the warring mountains were several great peaks: Tongariro, the proud and fierce; Pihanga, the beautiful; and Taranaki, the jealous. Taranaki loved Pihanga and fought to possess her, but Tongariro was stronger and drove Taranaki back. The battle was terrible—rivers of fire flowed from their flanks, clouds of ash darkened the sky, and the earth shook with their fury.

At last, the gods intervened. Rongo, the god of peace and cultivated food, commanded the mountains to cease their fighting. He decreed that each mountain must take its place and remain forever still. Tongariro was given the central position and the hot springs that still steam from his flanks. Pihanga stood serene beside him. And Taranaki was banished to the west, where he stands alone and beautiful, weeping rivers that flow to the sea.

The story explains the geography of the central North Island: Tongariro's many craters and hot springs are the wounds from the ancient battle, and Taranaki's perfect volcanic cone stands apart from the other mountains, forever separated from the one he loved. On still evenings, the people say, Taranaki's shadow still reaches across the plains toward Pihanga, a love that distance could not extinguish.
story1365:
Tangaroa and Tane were brothers, but they were brothers of fundamentally different temperaments. Tangaroa was the god of the sea—restless, deep, and cold. Tane was the god of the forest—still, green, and full of life. In the beginning, they shared dominion over all things, but jealousy grew between them.

Tangaroa desired the trees of Tane's forest, for the wood of trees could be carved into canoes that would carry his people across his ocean. But Tane refused to give his trees to the sea god, for the trees were his children and he would not see them drowned. The brothers quarreled, and their quarrel became a war.

Tangaroa sent great waves to crash against the shore, tearing trees from the land and dragging them into the sea. Tane sent his roots deeper into the earth and his branches higher into the sky, refusing to yield. The forests fought back—branches became spears, roots became anchors, and the battle raged across the boundary between land and sea.

At last, Rongo intervened and set a boundary: the sea would have its domain, the forest its own, and where they met at the shore would be a place of both destruction and creation. Tides would erode the land, but the land would resist. Trees would fall into the sea, but their wood would become the canoes that carried humans between the islands.

This is why, the Maori say, the sea and the forest are forever enemies and allies. The tide eats the shore, but the trees hold the soil. The waves tear down, but the forest builds up. In their eternal struggle, they create the coastline—ever-changing, ever-creating, the meeting place of two great gods who cannot live without each other.
